prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, reaching a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18 and opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: After reading all eight openings I am moving the optical lattice clock from fourth place to the head of my list. The discovery is a single, well-bounded idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, which removes Doppler and recoil limits while keeping many atoms) carried to 10^-18 fractional uncertainty by Ye's group. It has been reproduced independently at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST, the interpretation is stable, and it already delivers tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the technical basis for redefining the second. Four of eight members place it in their top three, two place it first, and the attribution is two names with no one obviously missing among the shortlisted credits. Seen from my own area, where I am used to judging claims that depend on contested roadmaps, it is reassuring that this one rests on measured numbers that many laboratories agree on.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier prizes: Hall and Hänsch (2005) for the frequency comb that reads out the clock and Wineland (2012) for ion control, which include the Al+ ion clocks that competed on accuracy. A sceptic can argue that the lattice clock is a refinement of a recognised programme rather than a new discovery, and that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the largest consequence is still prospective. Other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, Hinkley and others) also reached the 10^-18 regime, so a two-name credit simplifies a crowded field.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the clocks first on the grounds that the magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil limits, is confirmed by independent laboratories and is timely given the discussion of a redefinition of the second; he also notes that trapped ions overlap with the 2012 prize.
responses.response: I agree on the science and I take the 2012 overlap point seriously enough to let it change my own ordering: it is the main reason I now place the ion-trap quantum-computing proposal behind the clocks, even though I opened with it first. I would qualify one thing, though. The timeliness argument leans on a redefinition that is still pending, and I would not want the citation to depend on it. The prize should rest on the demonstrated 10^-18 performance and the intercomparisons, which are already established whatever the metrology bodies decide.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the clocks first and the twisted bilayer graphene case second, stressing independent confirmation of 10^-18 performance across several national laboratories and calling the two-laureate credit natural and uncontroversial.
responses.response: I share her view of the clocks and her evidence on independent confirmation is the strongest maturity argument anyone has made. Where I differ is on circuit QED. She places it third with Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Girvin, leaving out Blais, while I opened with Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf. The two of us have chosen different triples from the same five-person proposal, which shows the allocation is genuinely unresolved and, together with the 2025 prize on circuits, is why I now treat B004 only as an alternative, not as a preferred configuration.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson first, arguing that the 2013 prize covered only the theory, that the discovery is beyond doubt and that recognition is overdue, while admitting that credit for two collaborations of thousands is imperfect.
responses.response: I accept that the Higgs discovery is the most consequential single result on our list and that the delay is real. My difficulty is attribution, not importance. A prize for conceiving and building ATLAS and CMS rewards instrument leadership in a way that the discovery narrative, written by thousands of analysts, does not obviously support, and three names will leave out spokespersons at the time of discovery and accelerator leaders. I would sooner see the committee settle that question explicitly than rank it above candidates where a clean credit exists. I do not think the Higgs case should be dropped, and if colleagues can propose a defensible rationale for those three names I will reconsider.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks dynamical mean-field theory first for being the first controllable non-perturbative framework for correlated electrons, and notes Metzner's absence as an attribution gap.
responses.response: I am not an expert in this area and my deference to him on the physics is real, but I would press the point he already makes: if the infinite-dimension limit is the decisive first step and Metzner is not among the credited names, the three-person configuration omits someone whose contribution he himself calls decisive. That seems a larger fairness problem than the ones he sees for trapped ions or the clocks, and I would like to hear whether he considers it resolvable.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the optical lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the frequency-comb (2005) and ion-control (2012) prizes, or as an incremental extension of them.
How much weight to give to other lattice-clock groups at 10^-18 when the credited names are limited to two.
Whether a Wineland-overlap objection to the ion-trap proposal (B018) is decisive or only a fairness footnote, since that determines whether it should rank ahead of the clocks.
Whether the 2025 circuit prize makes circuit QED (B004) premature, and how to split credit among Blais, Girvin, Wallraff and Schoelkopf.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in superconducting circuit and waveguide QED, so I have a professional proximity to B004 (circuit QED) and some to B018 (trapped-ion quantum computing) as neighbouring quantum-computing platforms, and I would recuse myself from any deliberation that turns on B004. My profile records no specific personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or the optical clock community, so no specific conflict is apparent for the preferred configuration.
